metadata.title: U.S. kindergarten vaccine coverage falls, CDC says

sources.news_title: Vaccination Rates Largely Unchanged Among Kindergartners: CDC
sources.text:
Vaccination coverage among kindergartners remained about the same as before, according to new estimates released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Aug. 17.
The percentage of kindergartners who have received a vaccine against hepatitis B stayed at 94 percent, according to data collected by states and the District of Columbia in late 2025 and early 2026 and passed on to the CDC before being reported on Monday.
Coverage of three other vaccines declined slightly, by 0.1 percent. Some 92.4 percent of kindergartners had received a measles, mumps, rubella shot; 92 percent had received a vaccine against diphtheria and tetanus; and 92.4 percent had received a vaccine against polio.
For vaccination against chickenpox, or varicella, the percentage of kids who had a history of two doses was about the same, at 92.2 percent. The percentage who had received two doses declined by 0.6 percent, to 93.4 percent.
At the same time, exemptions from vaccines, which can be obtained on a medical or religious basis depending on state law, increased from 3.6 percent to 4.2 percent. That amounted to 155,000 kindergartners with an exemption to one or more vaccines.
The new data show that vaccination rates among kindergartners “remained high,” the CDC said in an Aug. 17 statement. “CDC continues to encourage parents to discuss vaccination options with their doctors,” the public health agency said.
The CDC releases the kindergarten vaccine estimates annually. The agency’s database has coverage estimates dating back to late 2011. Hepatitis B vaccination coverage peaked at 96.4 percent in 2011 and 2012. Measles vaccination peaked at 95.2 percent in 2019 and 2020. Diphtheria and tetanus vaccination was the highest in 2016, 2017, and 2018, at 95.2 percent. Polio vaccination was 95.3 percent in 2011 and 2012, a high not seen since.
The highest coverage for one-dose chickenpox vaccination was in 2018 and 2019 (94.3 percent), and two-dose chickenpox vaccination was in 2016 and 2017 (97.5 percent).
Rates for vaccines against, among other diseases, influenza and pneumococcal disease are not included in the estimates.
The CDC issues a recommended vaccine schedule, which has traditionally been adopted with little or no change by states. The CDC began changing some vaccine recommendations in 2025 under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., prompting some states to diverge from its schedule.
Some outside groups, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, which receives money from vaccine companies, have criticized the changes, saying they would result in lower vaccination coverage and higher rates of disease.
The academy did not respond to The Epoch Times’ request for comment by time of publication.
“The latest figures continue a broader decline that took hold under the Biden administration during the COVID-19 pandemic, as mandates, shifting guidance, and the administration’s mishandling of pandemic-era vaccination policy eroded public trust in health institutions,” a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, the CDC’s parent agency, told The Epoch Times in an email.
The department “continues to encourage parents to make informed decisions about protecting their children from infectious, vaccine-preventable diseases,” the spokesperson said.

sources.news_title: U.S. school vaccination rates inch down yet again and exemptions reach record high
US school vaccination rates inch down yet again and exemptions reach record high
sources.text:
US school vaccination rates inch down yet again and exemptions reach record high
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. kindergarten vaccination rates inched down again last year and the share of children with exemptions rose to an all-time high, according to federal data posted Monday.
The fraction of kids exempted from vaccine requirements rose to 4.2%, up from 3.6% the year before. That’s an estimated 155,000 children nationally during the 2025-2026 school year.
It’s the fourth consecutive year that the national average exemption rate has reached a new record, and the vast majority are parents withholding shots for nonmedical reasons. Exemptions increased in 41 states and the District of Columbia.
Experts point to turmoil caused by federal health officials.
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the antivaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of federal health agencies. In the last 18 months, Kennedy and other federal officials have repeatedly tried to revise and reduce childhood vaccination guidance. Earlier this month, Trump called for revamped childhood vaccination recommendations that promote his discredited theory that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
“The root cause of this is primarily because there’s so much chaos and confusion in vaccination recommendation systems in the last year or so,” said Dr. James Campbell, of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Vaccination rates fell for many diseases
The CDC reported that 92.4% of 2025-26 kindergarteners got their required measles-mumps-rubella shots, down slightly from the previous year. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the vaccination rate was 95% — the level that makes it unlikely that a single infection will spark a disease cluster or outbreak.
Vaccination rates also fell for polio, for the combination shot against diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis, and for the first dose of the vaccine against chickenpox.
The rate held steady for protection against hepatitis B. But that’s a vaccine given shortly after birth, and it will take a few years before recent federal efforts to upend infant hepatitis B vaccine recommendations would appear in the vaccination rates of kindergartners, Campbell said.
The vaccination numbers were posted as the U.S. experiences its worst year for measles since 1991.
The numbers indicate that more than a quarter of a million children entering kindergarten are susceptible to measles, said Campbell, a University of Maryland researcher who is chair of the AAP’s infectious diseases committee.
Those at-risk kids are not evenly distributed — concentrations of unvaccinated children are higher in some places than others, which helps explain why measles waves vary in intensity.
This is when public health officials typically tout vaccines’ benefits
The CDC data is coming out as school and health officials across the country are encouraging parents to get their children vaccinated as the school year starts.
“Back-to-school season is an important reminder that protecting our children’s health is both a shared responsibility and a shared goal,” North Carolina Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai said in a statement. “Vaccines help keep our children and teens healthy and in the classroom.”
In the past, the CDC has released the vaccination coverage data in its flagship publication, the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. CDC officials usually speak to the trends and stress the importance of vaccinations.
But since the Trump administration took office early last year, the agency has posted the data online. This year, the agency issued a three-sentence statement that noted a small decline in vaccination coverage among children entering kindergarten and said: “CDC continues to encourage parents to discuss vaccination options with their doctors.”
Medical exemption rates are steady
Public health officials focus on vaccination rates for kindergartners because schools can be cauldrons for germs and launching pads for community outbreaks.
For years, those rates were high, thanks largely to school attendance mandates that required key vaccinations. All U.S. states and territories require that children attending childcare centers and schools be vaccinated against a number of diseases, including measles, mumps, polio, tetanus, whooping cough and chickenpox.
All states allow exemptions for children with medical conditions that prevent them from receiving certain vaccines. And most also permit exemptions for religious or other nonmedical reasons.
In the last decade, the percentage of kindergartners with medical exemptions has held steady, at about 0.2%. But the percentage with nonmedical exemptions has risen.
According to the CDC data, 17.5% of kindergartners had an exemption to one or more vaccines in Idaho in the last school year. But fewer than 0.5% did in Connecticut.
___

sources.news_title: Kindergarten vaccine exemptions jump to another record high
CDC: U.S. kindergarten vaccine exemptions hit record high as coverage falls nationwide
sources.text:
CDC: U.S. kindergarten vaccine exemptions hit record high as coverage falls nationwide
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Vaccine exemptions among U.S. kindergarteners hit a new high in the 2025-2026 school year, rising to 4.2% as vaccination coverage slipped for every childhood vaccine tracked nationally, according to new CDC-reported data.
The exemption rate climbed from 3.6% the previous school year, a jump that translates to about 155,000 kindergarteners with exemptions from one or more required vaccines. The increase was widespread: exemption rates rose in 41 states and Washington, D.C.
At the same time, vaccination coverage declined across the board. National coverage ranged from 92.0% for DTaP to 92.4% for MMR and polio. Coverage for MMR, DTaP, polio and varicella fell in more than half of states.
The data also show gaps beyond formal exemptions. About 280,000 kindergarteners attended school without documentation that they had completed the MMR vaccine series.
Overall kindergarten vaccination coverage declined by about 0.1 percentage point from the previous school year. Public health officials often cite the need for very high vaccination coverage - roughly 95% for measles - to limit outbreaks, and the new figures show nearly half of states now above a 5% exemption rate, a level that can increase the risk of clusters of under-vaccinated children where outbreaks spread more easily.
The latest numbers underscore that the shift is not limited to a handful of places: exemptions reached a record high and increased across most of the country as routine childhood vaccination coverage continued to lose ground.
